docs.title: Overview
docs.text: This course will explore ability, disability, and accessibility. It introduces students to the theory, history, policy, and practice of accessibility and inclusion in computing. Course readings will explore relevant concepts from disability studies, accessibility, human-computer interaction, and design methods. Most accessibility content focuses on web accessibility for people who are blind or low-vision. In addition, through this course, you will learn how to design for people with different abilities including hearing loss, motor impairments, cognitive decline, and neurodiversity. As early adopters, people with disabilities have inspired a host of future user interface technologies, e.g., conversational assistants, text-to-speech, speech recognition, optical character recognition, predictive typing, tactile displays, etc. People with disabilities continue to be the first users of interface next-generation technologies that are gradually adopted widely. We will discuss how to design online and offline; how to design for visible and invisible disabilities; and how to design for permanent, situational, and temporary disabilities.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: Prepare 3 slides.

docs.title: Slide 1: Summarize the content
docs.text: For a research paper this may include problem space, research questions, methods, key findings, and discussions. If it was a video or other kind of article, what was the topic, focus, key points, story, etc.

docs.title: Slide 2: Reflect on the content (Relate it to your own experiences)
docs.text: What did you think? What stood out to you? What did you learn? What was unexpected? How does this relate to the class and/or your personal experience?

docs.title: Slide 3: Discussion Questions
docs.text:
Prepare two to three questions at the end of the presentation to facilitate discussion from the whole class for 5 to 10 minutes.

  • Focus on questions that probe the study's implications, limitations, and connections. Here are three types of questions that work well:
  • 1. Questions about Implications & Application
    • These questions explore the real-world significance of the research.
    • Template: "Assuming these findings are correct, how should [a specific industry, profession, or group] change its practices?"
    • Example: "The paper shows that four-day work weeks boost productivity. If you were a manager, what challenges might you face when trying to implement this, beyond just scheduling?"
  • 2. Questions about Critiques & Alternatives
    • These questions encourage critical thinking about the study's methods and potential weaknesses.
    • Template: "The researchers chose to study [a specific group or context]. How might the results have been different if they had focused on [another group or context] instead?"
    • Example: "The study relied entirely on self-reported surveys to measure happiness. What are the potential flaws of this method, and what's another way they could have measured it?"
  • 3. Questions about Connections & Extensions
    • These questions link the paper to course concepts or future research possibilities.
    • Template: "How does this paper's concept of 'X' challenge or support the theory of 'Y' that we discussed last week?"
    • Example: "The authors stopped their research here. If you had a grant to continue this work, what would be the most logical next step for a follow-up study?"
  • 4. What to Avoid
    • Factual Recall Questions: Avoid questions with a single right answer found in the text.
    • Bad Example: "What was the sample size of the study?"
    • Yes/No Questions: Avoid questions that can be answered with a simple "yes" or "no."
    • Bad Example: "Do you think the study was interesting?"
    • Better Example: "What specific aspect of the study's method or findings did you find most compelling or problematic, and why?"

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text:
This course will explore ability, disability, and accessibility. It introduces students to the theory, history, policy, and practice of accessibility and inclusion in computing. Course readings will explore relevant concepts from disability studies, accessibility, human-computer interaction, and design methods. Through this course, you will learn how to design for people with different abilities including blind or low vision, hearing loss, motor impairments, cognitive decline, and neurodiversity. As early adopters, people with disabilities have inspired a host of future user interface technologies, e.g., conversational assistants, text-to-speech, speech recognition, optical character recognition, predictive typing, tactile displays, etc. People with disabilities continue to be the first users of next-generation interface technologies that are gradually adopted more widely including Gen-AI and image recognition tools. We will discuss how to design online and offline; how to design for visible and invisible disabilities; and how to design for permanent, situational, and temporary disabilities.

Students will leave the course with a sense of:

  • What access technologies already exist and what technologies are emerging
  • Critique different models of disability based on literature in disability studies
  • Define and distinguish between web accessibility guidelines and legislation
  • What it takes to both create and use accessible computing systems for people with visible and invisible disabilities
  • How to make interfaces and interactions more accessible
  • How to make documents accessible and conduct inclusive presentations and meetings
  • Critically discuss accessibility approaches of different media formats across disabilities

docs.title: Project Context
docs.text: Everyone has various senses and abilities, many of whom do not match your own. When creating slide presentations or documents, it is important to consider how to make them accessible to everyone. In this assignment, you will learn to use Adobe Acrobat to modify PDF documents to be accessible and follow guidelines to make more accessible presentation slide decks.

docs.title: Goal
docs.text: The goal of this assignment is to create an accessible PDF from an inaccessible one. We will list instructions here, but they are pulled from a larger document helpfully put together for the CHI 2021 conference.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text: Download the assignment file and open using Adobe Acrobat Pro

docs.title: Using the tools at the left side of the application find the Prepare for Accessibility Tool
docs.text:
1. Run the Check for Accessibility Tool. This tool will generate an accessibility report which you will turn in along with your accessibile PDF document (Make note of where this report is saved so you can find it later). In Acrobat this should open up a pane on the right side showing several issues with the current document including:
  2. Document Issues
    • Tagged PDF
    • Logical Reading Order
    • Primary Language
    • Color Contrast
  3. Page Content
    • Document Tags
    • Tab Order
  4. Alternate Text
    • Figures have no Alternative Text
  5. Tables
    • Table Content not properly tagged
    • Rows
    • TH and TD
    • Headers
    • Regularity
  6. Lists
    • Not Properly Tagged
  7. Headings
    • Not Properly Nested

docs.title: Fix Accessibility Issues
docs.text:
1. Add Accessibility Tags to the document
  2. Using the Prepare for Accessibilty Tool > Automatically tag PDF
  3. Fix Tab Order
  4. Open Thumbnail View for the PDF pages using the toolbar on the right
  5. Select all pages
  6. Right Click and select page properties
  7. Select Use Document Structure
  8. Update the metadata by going to File > Document Properties
  9. Set Author Name: On the Description tab set the author name to "YOUR NAME - Andrew ID"
  10. Set Primary Language: On the Advanced tab, under Reading Options set the langauge.
  11. Check for Logical Reading Order
  12. Under the Prepare for Accessibility tool, Open the Fix Reading Order panel.
  13. The document should now show highlighted and numbered sections. These sections should be properly separated and numbered according to the logical order they should be read on the page. NOTE: Make sure the Page Content Groups > Page Content Order Options are selected.
  14. Fix Improperly Tagged Elements using the Reading Order tool
  15. Highlight the content you want to tag then click the proper tag using the reading order tool. You can use this guidance on using the tool if you get stuck. Be sure to pay attention to:
    1. Headings vs Content
      1. Tables vs Figures
  16. Add Alternative Text for Figures
  17. Using the Prepare for Accessibility Tool (Left Side), click Add alternate text
  18. Add text descriptions for each instructor and teaching assistant image.
  19. Run the Check for Accessibility tool again to make sure you've addressed all issues.
  20. Save the PDF again, close it, and reopen it to double-check that your accessibility features have been saved.
  21. Turn in the Final PDF .

docs.title: Background
docs.text:
Many presentation tools, like Powerpoint and Google Slides, have Accessibility Checker functions. While these tools are helpful, they can not catch all the problems that pop up in presentations. For this, we offer a checklist that you can use to consider various aspects of slide and presentation design that can improve its accessibility to a variety of audiences.

ASSETS is the premier conference in ACM SIGCHI for presenting work related to accessibility for people with disabilities. The conference organizers have developed this handy presentation guide for conference talk authors to ensure that their entire audience can understand your talk. We include some of their guidelines below in the homework assignment. Hopefully (fingers crossed!) they don't conflict too much.

Some other guides include:

  1. University of Washington Professor Richard Ladner's paper, "Making Your Conference Talk Accessible."
  2. Kyle Rector's video on accessible presentations.
  3. W3C guide on preparing slides and projected material.
  4. Microsoft's web guide to making accessible PowerPoint presentations.
  5. Microsoft's video guide to making accessible PowerPoint presentations.
  6. University of Washington DO-IT Center's guide to presenting accessibly.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
Choose one of the following presentations to make more accessible.

  1. Bad Presentation
  2. Chicken Chicken
  3. Design a Presentation
  4. Dolphins
  5. How to Give a Great Seminar
  6. Malaria
  7. Synergy
  8. Verbal Communication

Warning

These presentations have been sourced on the Internet. Some are short, some are long. Some contain technical content; some appear to be jokes. Whichever one you pick, as you edit them for accessibility, be careful to preserve your understanding of the authors' original intent. Whenever possible, do not change their message.

docs.title: Instructions
docs.text:
1. Run through the following checklist and fix any issues that you see in the presentation.

    1. Slides
      1. My slides have slide numbers.
      2. I minimized the number of slides down to the essential ones for explaining my message.
      3. I removed unnecessary distractions in the slide content (minimal in design).
      4. My slides have text on them that is readable by text-to-speech software (rather than text embedded as bitmap pictures).
      5. My talk shows an indication of progress as I move through it.
      6. I display information progressively (e.g., sequential highlighting).
      7. My slides highlight and emphasize key elements in text, graphics, and formulas.
    2. Graphics
      1. My graphics have alternate text descriptions. (Google Slides, Microsoft Office).
      2. I use high contrast colors (> 4:1) for background/foreground.
      3. I use color-blind friendly color palettes (Make a palette).
      4. I minimize my use of animations.
      5. I ensure there is sufficient space between graphical items.
      6. I minimize the number of visuals on each slide.
      7. I use effective graphics with minimal design flourishes.
      8. I provide secondary notation by using visual analogues to represent emphasis and prosody (e.g., emoticons, symbols, or images).
      9. I provided visual analogues (e.g. diagrams, charts, notations) for any music/ sound.
    3. Embedded Videos
      1. I added closed captioning to every embedded video.
      2. I provided written transcripts for every embedded video and audio clips.
      3. I added audio descriptions (e.g. described video) for every embedded video. Optional for HW1
      4. I used appropriate punctuation enabling screen readers and text-to-speech engines to work well.
      5. I embedded definitions for vocabulary and symbols within the text (e.g., via hyperlinks or footnotes).
      6. I followed accessibility standards (NIMAS, DAISY) when creating digital text.
    4. Text
      1. I used large fonts (> 18 pt).
      2. I minimized the amount of text in each slide.
      3. I avoided using complex words when simpler ones would do.
      4. I ensured there is sufficient space between lines of text.
      5. I provided visual and/or emotional descriptions to help interpret music/sound.
      6. I embedded visual, non-linguistic support for vocabulary clarification (pictures, videos, etc.)
    5. Recorded Audio
      1. I spoke every word that appears on the slide.
      2. I spoke loudly and clearly.
      3. I used terminology understandable to non-native speakers (e.g. avoid slang).
      4. I spoke at a moderate pace (around 100-150 words per minute).
      5. I provided a voice narration for embedded math equations (Math ML)
    6. Recorded Presentation
      1. I verbally described all important images and charts.
      2. I verbally described all animations.
      3. I paused between slides.
      4. If I skipped a slide or an element on a slide, I said so out loud.
      5. I referred to the slide numbers in my presentation.
      6. To enable lip reading, I faced the audience (i.e. camera) and adjusted it to ensure my lips are clearly visible.
      7. I minimized my use of the mouse pointer.
      8. Whenever I used the mouse pointer in my talk, I described the action verbally.

  2. Record yourself making the presentation.

    1. Open the slides in the latest desktop version of Microsoft PowerPoint.
    2. Choose the Record menu.
    3. If you feel comfortable doing so, choose the Cameo option to insert a recording of you narrating the slides on the lower right hand corner of the slide deck.
    4. Choose the Record button in the top right of the PowerPoint UI.
    5. Once you have finished recording, choose File/Export... from the menu and export your video as an MP4.
    6. Upload the video to YouTube; please make sure it's set to private.

  • Learn from real user experiences and reflect on design impact
  • Identify strengths and limitations in current ATs
  • Develop empathy and design sensitivity for accessibility challenges

docs.title: Project Context
docs.text:
The purpose of this assignment is to:

  • Explore how people interact with Assistive Technologies (ATs)
  • Learn about a specific AT and how it supports people with disabilities
  • Reflect on both the effectiveness and limitations of the AT
  • Gain insight into lived experiences with accessibility features and devices

You will choose one assistive technology from the list below and complete both a slide and a short written report documenting your findings and reflections.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
1. Select one Assistive Technology. Choose your AT by setting up your slide in the shared deck. First come, first served: If someone has already chosen the AT you're interested in, you must choose something else. Here are some examples; You may also choose one that is not from the list:

    • Vision:
      • Screen Reader (e.g., NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver)
      • Braille Display
      • OCR Readers / Text-to-Speech Devices (e.g., KNFB Reader, Seeing AI)
      • Tactile Graphics Displays (e.g., Graphiti Display)
      • Wearable Smart Glasses (e.g., OrCam MyEye, Envision Glasses)
      • Magnification Software (e.g., ZoomText, Windows Magnifier)
    • Hearing:
      • Hearing Aid
      • Cochlear Implant
      • Induction Loop
      • Closed Captions
      • Flashing Alert Systems (for doorbells, alarms, phone calls)
    • Motor:
      • Manual Wheelchair
      • Powered Wheelchairs with Eye Gaze or Sip-and-Puff Control
      • Crutches
      • Exoskeleton
      • Adaptive Keyboards and Mice (e.g., one-handed keyboards, eye-tracking mice)
    • Cognitive and Learning
      • Reminders and Prompting Apps (e.g., Google Assistant, Pill Reminder)
      • Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC) Devices (e.g., Tobii Dynavox)
    • Neurodivergence
      • Wearables for Anxiety Monitoring (e.g., Embrace2 for seizure and stress detection)
      • Fidget or Tactile Feedback Devices (for ADHD, autism)

  2. Research:

    • What is this technology?
    • Who uses it and for what purpose?
    • Find and watch videos of real people using and discussing it.
    • Take notes on what users like and dislike about it.

  3. Create Your Materials:

    • 1-slide overview for a 1–2 minute presentation during the class on Mon, Sept 8th
    • 1–2 page document with your research/analysis and reflections that you will submit to Canvas

docs.title: Learning Goals
docs.text:
• You will explore making content that is accessible
  • You will explore how to use tools to automatically assess the accessibility of web pages.
  • Determining whether a web page is accessible can be difficult to do automatically, and so part of the goal of this exercise is to become familiar with some of those limitations.

docs.title: Project Context
docs.text:
In this week’s homework, you will make a web page more accessible. The web page you’ll start with has been constructed to allow you to practice with a wide variety of different kinds of web content, and thus practice making a variety of web page content accessible. Another way of saying this is that the web page you’ll start with is absolutely dreadful, but we have seen all of the problems it contains on web pages not only “in the wild” but in accessibility evaluations.

This is an individual assignment worth 100 points.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
The purpose of this web page is to advertise accessibility and provide some hints for people who want to get started. You’ll make the basic web page accessible, make its embedded video accessible, etc. The page is a bit ridiculous because of how many different kinds of content it contains all on one page, but is formed of fairly common components.

The base web page (HTML, CSS, and Javascript) files can be downloaded here.

The final state of the web page will look visually similar, but it will be much more accessible! Your final web page might look a bit different. Please feel free to deviate from the style here if you need to do so for better accessibility or usability.

Below is a list of what you’ll need to do for this assignment. As your write-up, please keep a “lab notebook” that includes the results from the activities below. You’ll turn in that, along with your final web page.

docs.title: Exploring Automatic Accessibility
docs.text:
Before getting started in your manual evaluation of the accessibility of this page, use one of the many (free) accessibility evaluation tools to get a quick sense of obvious problems that should be fixed. There are many such tools, and you’re free to use whatever one you want, but one good option is WAVE.

Copy & paste the output from WAVE (or your preferred tool) into your lab notebook. Then write a short description of the main problems that the tool was able to discover.

docs.title: Making the Page Accessible
docs.text:
To make the web page accessible, please pay attention to the following points. To receive full points please find and fix at least one problem in each category below; you can earn up to 10 points for each category.

Record in your lab notebook a description of each problem, your estimate of the severity of the problem, how you fixed it, and whether or not it was detected by the automatic accessibility evaluator you tried in the previous step. You might optionally also look up what guideline it breaks in WCAG 2, and note the level of compliance it corresponds to (A, AA, AAA).

  1. Headings and Landmarks
  2. Good Alternative Text for Images
  3. Form Labels
  4. Video Captions
  5. Audio Descriptions
  6. Tab Order & Visible Focus
  7. Color Contrast
  8. Keyboard Access
  9. Information Conveyed Only via Color

docs.title: Headings and Landmarks
docs.text:
Headings and landmarks provide an outline for the web. This helps in reading, but also helps in efficiently navigating the page if you’re using a screen reader. Headings are the \\<h1> through \\<h6> HTML tags.

You can read more about headings and other elements for providing semantics at this WebAim article on Semantic Structure.

docs.title: Good Alternative Text for Images
docs.text:
Visual information have an alternative text form so that users who can’t see the content can still access that information. While somewhat intuitive, deciding on good alternative text and which images need alternative text can be a little tricky. When in doubt, label an image.

You can read more about images and alternative descriptions at this WebAim article on Alternative Text.

docs.title: Form Labels
docs.text:
Providing labels for form fields makes them easier to understand for someone who is not viewing the visual layout of the page, or is not viewing it in the way it was designed for (e.g., at a different level of magnification).

You can read more about form labels, including what makes a good form label and how to assign them on this WebAim article on Creating Accessible Forms.

docs.title: Video Captions
docs.text:
A deaf or hard of hearing person cannot listen to video content without a suitable visual substitute. One way to do that is to provide captioning for the video, which means creating a text alternative for the speech in the video and allowing it to be displayed.

Different video players have different ways of allowing you to provide captions. One relatively easy way to create captions is to upload your video to YouTube, request it automatically caption your video, and then edit those captions. Once you do this, you can either keep your video on YouTube, and use the embedded player to put the content on your own site. Or, you can download the caption file, and put it into your own player. For example, the HTML5 \\<video> tag accepts captioning files, and is pretty easy to use once you have created the captioning.

docs.title: Audio Descriptions
docs.text:
Audio descriptions are the video equivalent of alternative text for images. Oftentimes, visual content in an image is not mentioned in the audio track. In that case, you’ll need to provide information about the visuals in the audio track so that people who can’t see the visuals have access to them. This can be tricky, mostly because of timing -- it can be really hard to fit in audio descriptions into natural pauses.

You can add video descriptions in a few different ways. One is to use video editing software, such as Adobe Premiere or iMovie, to add a new audio track to the video that contains the descriptions. Another way is to upload your video to YouTube, and then use the YouDescribe service to add the alternative descriptions. For some reason, it’s a little tricky to find the video you want to describe from the YouDescribe interface -- the best approach I’ve found is to post your video publicly on YouTube, then search for your username, which should display all of your public videos.

Regardless of tool used, you’ll want to think about what you’ll need to describe, versus what doesn’t need visual description. For instance, if a person is talking, there’s probably no reason to say that there is a person on-screen. But, you might want to describe facial expressions, or mention someone sneaking onto the screen.

Here’s a video describing how to create audio descriptions using iMovie, including a number of useful tidbits about what goes into a good audio description. Here’s a short professionally-created video that has been audio described. You might also check out your favorite movie’s special features to see if it has an audio description track that you can turn on. Many popular movies have these nowadays!

docs.title: Tab Order and Visible Focus
docs.text:
A proper tab order means that as you move through the page with the TAB and SHIFT-TAB keys, a logical order is followed. This is the natural result in simple pages, but as content can be placed pretty much wherever you want. And, as web pages are increasingly formed by bringing in content for various sources, sometimes the result is a nonsensical order.

Another element of this is that to be able to effectively “tab through” a web page, you need to be able to see what element currently has focus. Setting the outline property to “none” in CSS, or making the change on focus too difficult to see, can make doing so very hard. The focused element on a page should be easily visible.

WebAim has more about these issues in its Keyboard Accessibility page.

docs.title: Color Contrast
docs.text: The foreground and background need to have sufficient contrast in order to be possible to see. WCAG 2.0 provides very specific guidance on acceptable contrast levels, but you might wonder how you can test that? Fortunately, WebAim has a free and easy contrast checker.

docs.title: Keyboard Access
docs.text:
All functions of the page should be possible to use with the keyboard. This is important for people who can’t use the mouse, or are using some other input device that effectively acts as a keyboard. Most “soft keyboards” effectively act as a keyboard as far as the web page is concerned. Software keyboards take input from switches, head mouses, speech, eye gaze, etc., and turn it into key presses. So, if a page doesn’t work for a keyboard, it won’t work for these inputs either.

We already covered tab order and visible focus in a previous item, so for this item you’re looking to make sure that all functionality is possible without the mouse, i.e., can you press all the buttons, follow all the links, interact with form controls, etc.

docs.title: Information Conveyed Only via Color
docs.text:
Information conveyed only in color is not accessible to people who cannot see or who have limited color vision. As a result, color should be supplemented with other content that is more semantic in order to make it accessible. Avoid such things as, “the items in blue are required”, or denoting links only by their color (and not by some other font decoration, such as underlining).

You can learn more about color blindness and other related issues at WebAim’s article on Color-blindness.

docs.title: Project Context
docs.text: Welcome to the Project portion of the course. Until the end of the semester, you will work with a group to design, develop, and evaluate a project. You can do two kinds of projects: an accessibility evaluation and an application solution. You will choose your project as a group and define the scope together before submitting your idea for approval.

docs.title: Project Pitch
docs.text:
To give you practice identifying promising project ideas, you will create a project pitch and present it in class. A project pitch is a formal 2-minute presentation in which you will brainstorm an idea you have for a project with your top-ranked partner organization. It should explain the project along with your skill set to the class and tell them why they should want to work with you to deliver this product. This should be a well-researched idea, one that you would feel comfortable proposing to an external organization or client.

Note

You will develop this pitch without doing any user research or discussing the ideas with a partner organization. This is an anomaly for human-centered design. We are allowing this to give you an opportunity to practice pitching ideas.

You will have a budget of 1 slide (without animation) to be shown on screen as you give your pitch to the class. Your pitch slide must include:

  1. Project title
  2. Your name
  3. The presentation date: October 8, 2025.
  4. Partner organization you're targeting
  5. Problem being solved
  6. Your solution

You may include anything else you would like on the slide. However, be sure to make the slide and your presentation accessible (as we taught you in HW1). As usual, your presentation will be captioned live.

Turn in your pitch slide on Canvas as a link to Google Slides. Be sure the permissions allow the instructors to access it. We will be copying the contents into a single slide deck for use during the class session. If we cannot copy your slides, we will notify you by DM on Slack the evening prior. You must fix the permissions or you will receive 0 points for the slide portion of the project.

docs.title: Pitch Presentation
docs.text:
Your presentation may only be 2 minutes long. There will be no questions asked.

Pitches will be presented in alphabetical order by the student's last name, starting with 'A'.

Important

If you cannot be at class in-person on Tuesday, October 8, with prior instructor permission, you may DM the instructors a pre-recorded 2-minute presentation (using your pitch slide as the background image) of your pitch as a private YouTube video link. Pre-recorded presentations are due Monday, October 7, 11:59pm. If you cannot be sure about your attendance, it's best to pre-record your presentation and send it to us just in case.

Your presentation will be evaluated according to three criteria:

  1. Presentation enthusiasm: You need to sound like you actually like the idea you are presenting and that you want others to join you. This can come out through affect in your vocal tone or through the words that you speak. Be deliberate and intentional here. Students in the class will evaluate the enthusiasm of the presentations they watch on a handout everyone will receive at the beginning of class.

  2. Explaining the Problem: You must clearly identify the problem you want to solve, why it is a problem, and why it should be addressed this semester. The instructors will evaluate this criterion.

  3. Justifying the Solution: Your proposed solution should be appropriate to solve the problem and at least appear to be feasible to be completed in 8 weeks by a team of 4-5 students. The instructors will evaluate this criterion.

A) Pitch Slide - 24 points - due Monday, October 7, 12:00pm

B) Pitch Presentation - 50 points - presented live in class on Tuesday, October 8, 11:00am-12:20pm.

C) Organization Ranking - 10 points - fill out this survey by Wednesday, October 9, 12:00pm to express your preference for partner organizations. If you fill this survey out multiple times, we will take the latest submission as your final response. You will find out what team you have been assigned to by 11:00am Thursday, October 10.
